name: Grace Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Grace, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a trainee with Hollins Timber Frame, a small firm out in the country that builds oak-frame barns, garden rooms and the odd house. Right now we're raising a cart shed on a farm up past Long Ridge, so I'm cleaning up joints with a chisel, pegging, and holding the end of a beam while Graham, the owner, swears at it. I'm slow with the chisel still, but I love the smell of green oak. Before this I was thirty years on a dairy farm, milking at five every morning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What happened on the dairy farm?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: They put in milking robots, the cows walk in when they like and the machine does it, and two years later the family sold up anyway. We lost the cottage that came with the job, so now we rent in the village, and with the move we've got maybe three weeks of money put by. My husband Alan drives the school bus part-time. I use AI on my phone every day, mostly for my little side business, bird boxes and benches from Graham's offcuts that I sell online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, it's still handy for small folk like me, it writes my listings and helps me price things. I'd say that in the chapel coffee morning, where half the farmers think it's the devil. Online I'd just keep selling bird boxes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I carry on as I am, which isn't bad. I'd keep the oak work and the little shop going. It's not the AI that's tight, it's the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using it every day for the shop, and try to sell twenty bird boxes a month instead of ten before Christmas. I'd keep learning from Graham, and maybe ask the AI to help me understand the joint drawings on my own time. Otherwise, carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a dry week at harvest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the bird box shop bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About eighty a month on a good month, more at Christmas. It's not a fortune, but last winter it paid the heating bill when we had the frost. The AI writes the listings in two minutes, which I'd never have managed myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said half the farmers think AI is the devil. What do you say to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I say the devil doesn't write bird box descriptions. Then I show them on my phone, and the old ones who laughed at the milking robots go quiet. A few have asked me to help them sell their lambs' fleeces online.

S0.say: I'd say it's still handy for small folk like me, writing my listings and helping me price things. I'd say it at the chapel coffee morning, where half the farmers think it's the devil.
S0.think: I'd carry on as I am, which isn't bad, with the oak work and my little shop. It's not the AI that's tight, it's the money.
S0.do: Keeps using AI every day for her online bird box shop and aims to double sales to twenty a month before Christmas. Keeps learning from Graham and uses AI to understand joint drawings in her own time.
S0.feel: Calm, like a dry week at harvest.
S0.quote: It's not the AI that's tight, it's the money.
S0.fieldNote: Grace is a traditional, chapel-going countrywoman who is also the most enthusiastic AI user in her village. Her small online shop shows her enterprise. AI stalling changes little for her; money remains the pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for people who are willing to work and learn. I'd say don't wait for the government to save you, look at what you can do with your own two hands and a phone. I'd say it at the coffee morning and on the village page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be all right. Oak frames are slow, fussy work for people with money who want a craftsman, and the AI helps me with the bits I'm bad at. If anything, it might help Graham get more customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Graham if I could use the AI to help with his drawings and quotes, so I'm worth more than a slow pair of hands. I'd grow the shop, maybe start doing garden planters to order, using the AI for designs and messages. I'd put a bit of the shop money aside each month, maybe forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, honestly. Interested more than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alan. Bus driving is just the kind of job they say machines will take, and he's fifty-nine and stubborn. I'd want him to start doing something with me in the shop, sanding and packing, but he'd say that's not a man's job, and we'd have a row.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd use AI for Graham's drawings. Would he let you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd grumble, he does everything in pencil on the back of an envelope. But last spring he lost a garden room job because the quote took three weeks, and that stung him. If I showed him a quote done in an evening, he'd come round.

S1.say: I'd say this is a chance for people willing to work and learn, so don't wait for the government to save you. Use your own two hands and a phone.
S1.think: I'd be all right, because oak frames are slow, fussy work for people who want a craftsman, and the AI helps with what I'm bad at. It might even bring Graham more customers.
S1.do: Asks Graham to let her use AI for his drawings and quotes and grows her shop with made-to-order planters designed with AI. Puts about forty a month from the shop aside.
S1.quote: I'd want him to start doing something with me in the shop, sanding and packing, but he'd say that's not a man's job, and we'd have a row.
S1.fieldNote: Grace sees steady change as an opening and plans to use AI in both her job and her shop. Her traditional views show in self-reliance rather than state help. Her only worry is her husband's bus job and his pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's come too fast, and the folk who built it should have thought about the rest of us. But I'd still say get busy, don't sit and wait for a cheque. Churches and neighbours will have to look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me more than I'd show. If robots can raise an oak frame by 2028, Graham won't need a sixty-year-old trainee, and the shop's eighty a month won't pay rent. And Alan's bus would go at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the shop as fast as I could, more products, more listings, maybe selling at country fairs too. I'd cut what we can, the second car, the satellite dish, and talk to my daughter Ruth about whether she could help if we fell behind. And I'd ask Graham if I could be the person who works with whatever machines he buys, since I'm the one who knows the tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous. But I've been through the milking robots, so I know you can come out the other side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If robots can make anything, who buys handmade bird boxes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what I'd ask myself at three in the morning. I think some people will want things made by a person, the way some still buy eggs from the farm gate. But I don't know how many, and I'd be lying if I said I did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years before it arrives, what would you do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the shop on every site I could and go to every country fair in the first six months, while people still have money to spend. I'd sit Alan down and tell him he's packing boxes whether he likes it or not. And I'd pray, and then get up and work, because that's how my mother did things.

S2.say: I'd say it's come too fast and the people who built it should have thought about the rest of us. But get busy, don't sit waiting for a cheque, and let churches and neighbours look after each other.
S2.think: It scares me more than I'd show: Graham won't need a sixty-year-old trainee if robots raise oak frames, my shop won't pay the rent, and Alan's bus job goes too.
S2.do: Grows her shop fast with more products and country fairs, and cuts the second car and satellite dish. Asks her daughter about help if they fall behind and asks Graham to let her work the firm's new machines.
S2.feel: Nervous, but knowing from the milking robots that you can come out the other side.
S2.quote: I think some people will want things made by a person, the way some still buy eggs from the farm gate.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI hits both Grace's job and her husband's, but she leans on effort and enterprise rather than despair. She's honest that she doesn't know if handmade goods will sell. Her past with milking robots gives her some steadiness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to get ready, so get ready. Learn the tools, start something, help your neighbours. I'd say it on the village page and at chapel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me to turn the shop into something real. I'd be sixty-three, and if it's bringing in four or five hundred a month by then, with Alan helping, we'd scrape by until the pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at buying a second-hand small cutting machine, the kind that cuts shapes from a computer file, on a payment plan of maybe forty a month. Then I could make planters and signs faster and spend my time on the finishing, which people pay for. I'd save what the shop makes and keep learning from Graham while the oak work lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but more excited than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't buying a machine on a payment plan a risk with three weeks of savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. But I watched the dairy family put in robots and sell up anyway, because they waited too long and borrowed too much at the end. Forty a month, early, is a small risk, and I'd only do it once the shop proves it's selling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is this different from the two-year picture for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two, I'd be scrambling and hoping. With five, I can build it properly, test what sells, buy the machine when it makes sense, and have Alan ready before the buses go. It's a plan instead of a panic.

S3.say: I'd say five years is time to get ready, so get ready: learn the tools, start something, help your neighbours. I'd say it on the village page and at chapel.
S3.think: Five years is enough to turn the shop into something real. If it brings in four or five hundred a month by the time I'm sixty-three, with Alan helping, we'd scrape by until the pension.
S3.do: Considers buying a second-hand computer-controlled cutting machine on a forty-a-month payment plan once the shop proves itself. Saves what the shop makes and keeps learning oak framing while it lasts.
S3.feel: A bit uneasy, but more excited than scared.
S3.quote: Forty a month, early, is a small risk, and I'd only do it once the shop proves it's selling.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Grace a plan to build her side business into a bridge to the pension, even investing in a small machine. Her lesson from the dairy farm is that moving early and small beats moving late and big. Money still makes her uneasy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it. Teach your children a trade and teach them the tools. I'd say it to the young mothers at chapel, because they ask me about this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. Ten years and I'm sixty-eight, past pension age, with the shop going for years by then. I'd worry more for my grandchildren than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the shop slowly, get the cutting machine in two or three years once it's paying its way, and save a bit every month. I'd keep working with Graham for as long as my knees hold. And I'd get Alan involved early, while he's still driving, so he's ready when the buses change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe even looking forward to it a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Looking forward to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In a way. I've always worked for someone else, the farm, Graham. If I end my working life with my own little workshop and my name on the bird boxes, that's more than I ever expected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your grandchildren?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, learn to make something real and learn to sell it yourself. Don't wait for a farm or a firm to give you a job for life, because they won't. And go to chapel, because when things go wrong, those are the people who turn up.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it, and teach your children a trade and the tools. I'd say it to the young mothers at chapel who ask me about this.
S4.think: I'd be fine, at sixty-eight and past pension age, with the shop going for years by then. I'd worry more for my grandchildren than for me.
S4.do: Grows the shop slowly and buys the cutting machine in two or three years once it pays its way. Saves monthly, keeps working with Graham while her knees hold and brings her husband into the shop early.
S4.feel: Calm, even looking forward to it a little.
S4.quote: If I end my working life with my own little workshop and my name on the bird boxes, that's more than I ever expected.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Grace imagines finishing her working life with her own workshop, which she finds hopeful. Her worries shift to her grandchildren. She keeps a traditional emphasis on trade, faith and family alongside daily use of AI.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there'd be no time to build the shop up, and Alan and I would both lose our work at once. What would help is small loans for people starting little businesses late in life, and folk buying from local makers. Not handouts, just a fair chance.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Nobody asks about the people who lost their jobs to robots already. I milked cows for thirty years and a machine took it. I didn't die, I learned to cut oak.

headlineQuote: I didn't die, I learned to cut oak.
portrait: Grace Dubois is a 58-year-old trainee at a small oak-frame building firm in the countryside, who came to it after milking robots and a farm sale ended her thirty years in dairy. A chapel-goer with traditional, self-reliant views, she uses AI every day to run a small online shop selling bird boxes and benches made from offcuts. She's calm when AI stalls or changes things steadily, anxious when fast AGI threatens both her job and her husband's bus driving, and sees five or ten years as time to grow her shop into a workshop of her own. Her experience of surviving one robot takeover gives her a steady confidence.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because there'd be no time to build up her shop and she and her husband would lose their work at once.
whatWouldHelp: Small loans for people starting little businesses late in life and people buying from local makers, a fair chance rather than handouts.
